Daniel’s checklist usefully echoes a long tradition of “active skepticism” (Popper’s falsificationism in miniature, plus something like Pólya’s problem-solving heuristics), but the central blind spot is that he treats “generalize” as an unqualified virtue. In finance especially, the instinct to generalize is exactly where smart people blow up: relationships are regime-dependent, incentives mutate the data-generating process, and models often fail not because the logic is wrong but because the environment changes or the metric becomes a target (a version of [Goodhart’s law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodhart%27s_law)). A sharper framing would pair generalization with an explicit “boundary conditions / model risk” step: *what would have to stay stable for this to keep working, and what are plausible ways stability breaks?* That’s the difference between “portable insight” and “overfitting dressed as theory,” a distinction emphasized in different ways by [Kahneman & Tversky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow) (base-rate neglect, narrative coherence) and by Taleb’s critique of fragile inference in nonstationary domains ([*The Black Swan*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Black_Swan_(book))).

The O(1)/O(N) metaphor is clever but also misleading: critical thinking rarely has constant cost, and the real constraint for students is not asymptotic complexity but attention, incentives, and error consequences. A finance student should learn to *allocate skepticism*—what deserves a quick “sanity check” versus a full audit—using expected impact and reversibility (small stakes vs career-defining decisions). Daniel’s “offline pooling” idea points in that direction, yet it omits a key operational detail: without a mechanism (notes, spaced review, or explicit prediction logs), monthly reflection tends to become vague rumination rather than cumulative calibration. Adding even one concrete practice—e.g., writing a falsifiable prediction before accepting a claim, then tracking outcomes in the spirit of [Tetlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superforecasting)—would make the post’s advice not just philosophically sound but behaviorally executable.
